checks.group: SEC / Threat model and secret ownership
checks.scope: Library source, every target; Linux runtime
checks.method: Source trace of every secret from entry to wipe: `P_enc`, the phrase text, the entropy, the Feistel workspace, the Argon2id work area, the passphrase NFKD and the seed, the repair words, the check-word indexes and the draw's trial entropy; owners and copies; what `Debug` and the errors carry.
checks.evidence: No `Clone` on a secret holder, `Debug` hidden on all of them, errors carry counts, positions, settings and codes only; the heap test of password encoding and seed derivation passed in `security-cargo-test.log` (local).

checks.group: SEC / Isolation in place of vault, CSP and sandbox
checks.scope: Linux runtime; Android, macOS, iOS, Windows by reading
checks.method: The browser parts (vault, iframe, CSP, message port) do not exist in a library. In their place, `Isolation::enter()` on every system: tested on Linux in a one-thread process with the crate's tests and a kernel read-back harness; the seccomp program checked by hand against the x86-64 and AArch64 syscall tables; the other systems read against their documentation.
checks.evidence: Isolation probe: 22 PASS, 0 failed (`security-isolation-probe.log` (local), `record-isolation-probe.log` (local)); isolation tests 3 of 3. Non-Linux systems by reading and CI run 40492969676 only.

checks.group: SEC / Network egress and secret guards
checks.method: Search for network code; sockets and `io_uring` after `enter()`; Landlock refusal of `connect` on a socket opened before the call; the empty network namespace. Pattern guards at export boundaries are not applicable: the library has none.
checks.evidence: The only `std::net` use is the macOS read-back probe, which sends nothing; five socket families and `io_uring_setup` refused with `EACCES` (`security-isolation-probe.log` (local)).

checks.group: SEC / Randomness, encryption and authentication
checks.method: No random source in the lockfile, the source or `build.rs`; `draw` takes the host's fill through a 32-byte array. The unauthenticated Feistel construction, salts, masks, verifier, fixed-point refusal and creation check against specification 0.7.0 through the recorded-key replays; refusals before any Argon2id work.
checks.evidence: `security-no-rng.log` (local); `security-fixtures-vs-spec.log` (local): 35 fixture files identical to the specification's vectors; every round of every transcript replays in both directions (`security-cargo-test.log` (local)). Full-cost replay only in CI.

checks.group: SEC / Secret lifecycle and exceptional paths
checks.method: Every error and cancellation path drops and wipes its secrets; `stack::cleared` on `Ok` and `Err`; the work area wiped by the C code on success and by `ffi::run` on failure; no input-reachable panic; unwind from a host callback (out of scope, CORE-54).
checks.evidence: `security-argon2-stack.log` (local): the C wrapper leaves 0 non-zero stack bytes, the vendored code writes 6263 bytes deep against a 16384-byte clear; work-area wipe tests pass (`security-cargo-test.log` (local)).

checks.group: SEC / Browser injection, persistence and sensitive APIs
checks.method: Search of `src/` and `Cargo.toml` for output, file, environment and browser APIs.
checks.evidence: No browser, DOM, HTML, URL, storage, logs or dynamic code: the library prints nothing, writes no files and reads no environment; its only output is `protect::write_secret` on request. Library analogues hold (errors and `Debug` carry no secrets).

checks.group: SEC / Read-only guarantees and availability bounds
checks.method: Growth of time with input length for public entry points; refusal time of 64 MiB inputs; the worst repair search; limits on work factor and memory. Read-only and spending surfaces do not exist in the library.
checks.evidence: `security-input-bounds.log` (local): passphrase NFKD quadratic; 64 MiB refused by `Password::new` in 0.354 s and by `Phrase::read` in 0.123 s; worst `Repaired::of` 0.084 s.

checks.group: FUN / BIP39, entropy and seed interpretation
checks.method: Line-by-line comparison with the specification; an independent Python implementation on the official word list; literal BIP39 vectors; typed-phrase differential; every prefix of every word; `from_entropy` for 0 to 40 bytes; 2,000 random passphrase seeds.
checks.evidence: `protocol-harness-run.log` (local): 30 literal rows, 3,008 typed phrases, 31,169 word tokens, 123 entropy cases and 2,000 seeds match; `protocol-negative-controls.log` (local).

checks.group: FUN / HD derivation and every coin or profile
checks.method: Source and public API search for BIP32, extended keys, paths and secp256k1.
checks.evidence: The crate has no HD derivation: the wallet check stops at the 64-byte BIP39 seed; addresses for a rehearsal are the host's.

checks.method: Source and public API reading.
checks.evidence: None of these exist in the crate.

checks.group: FUN / Scripts, descriptors, Miniscript and multisig
checks.method: Source and public API reading.
checks.evidence: None of these exist in the crate.

checks.group: FUN / Transactions, PSBT and commitments
checks.method: Source and public API reading.
checks.evidence: None of these exist in the crate.

checks.group: FUN / Recovery and backup formats
checks.scope: Library; Python reference; CI full cost
checks.method: Both suites against the specification: packing, round messages, salts, masks, swaps, creation, the fixed point, recovery and its nine length branches, the admission table, `m(MEM)` and `t(PIM)`, MHFE-REPAIR-1 and MHFE-PASSWORD-CHECK-1. Vector replays and a seeded differential through the public API with a stand-in Argon2id.
checks.evidence: `protocol-harness-run.log` (local): 27 transcripts in both directions, 54 and 67 fast cases, 604 encryptions, 2,418 decryptions, 300 admission combinations, 4,400 cards, 4,805 repairs, 3,004 check-word cases and 41 draws match. Eight recovery cases need full cost: CI run 40471270163.

checks.group: FUN / Discovery, providers, proofs and accounting
checks.method: Source search for network and provider code.
checks.evidence: The crate reads no input and has no network or provider code; its socket references only refuse sockets.

checks.group: API / Actual dependency call contracts
checks.method: Each call into bip39 3.0.0, unicode-normalization 0.1.26, blake2 0.11.0, hmac 0.13.0, sha2 0.11.1, zeroize 1.9.1, libc 0.2.191, windows-sys 0.61.2 and the vendored Argon2 C code read against that version; probes with values outside the usual range.
checks.evidence: `api-probe-truncation.log` (local); `api-probe-nfkd-release.log` (local); every other call agrees with its contract.

checks.group: API / Async state, cancellation and revisions
checks.method: Every `ControlFlow` callback; the state after a `Break` and after each error; work-area reuse; reentrancy. Async, revision and UI parts do not exist in a synchronous library.
checks.evidence: `api-tests-lib-and-corpora.log` (local): cancellation at round 2, at `on_unchecked` and at decrypt round 5, then reuse; a failed call leaves the work area wiped.

checks.group: API / Public API contract (export schema not applicable)
checks.method: Rustdoc JSON against `docs/public-api.txt` and plan 3.2; `Debug` and `Display`; error traits; dependency types in signatures; `Send` and `Sync`; semver hazards; each public function on small thread stacks. CSV, JSON and XLSX exports do not exist.
checks.evidence: `api-public-surface-native.log` (local): 22 items, all checks pass; `api-probe-stack-floor-release.log` (local): 136 KiB needed.

checks.group: API / Encoding and interoperability
checks.method: An NFKD oracle from UnicodeData 18.0.0, checked against NormalizationTest 18.0.0; every scalar value and 200,000 random strings through `Password::new`; 2,000 passphrase seeds; UTF-8 strictness; word lists; the time of `Seed::derive` on growing passphrases. Hex, Base58, Base64, Bech32, CBOR, UR and QR do not exist in the crate.
checks.evidence: `protocol-harness-run.log` (local): 1,112,064 scalar values (67 refused, 310,274 accepted, 801,723 unassigned) and every other case match; `nfkd_cost.py` fails.

checks.group: BLD / Manifest, flags and feature composition
checks.method: Manifest, `build.rs`, lints, include list, toolchain; package list; `windows-sys` features one by one; the lowest allowed sha2 and zeroize; the crate has no features.

checks.group: BLD / Matrix depth and runtime sampling
checks.method: What each CI job runs and what it only compiles; planted Clippy violations in macOS-only code; repeated commands.
checks.evidence: `build-gh-ci-run-log.log` (local); `build-macos-clippy-gap.log` (local). Built but not run in CI: MinGW, Android, iOS, wasm32-unknown-unknown. Never built: see the limitations.

checks.group: BLD / Lockfiles, source provenance and licences

checks.group: BLD / Artifacts, CI and release workflows
checks.method: Pins, permissions, triggers, concurrency and shell interpolation of the three workflows; the release tag step; how Cargo treats a republished version; the code-rules gate with harnesses present. `cargo publish --dry-run` cannot run offline (CI ran it); the full-cost replay was not run locally.

checks.method: Inventory of the package and repository.

checks.group: ARC / Ownership, imports and composition seams

findings.title: Publishing other bytes as version 0.1.0 makes Cargo build the withdrawn 0.1.0 from its cache
findings.releaseBlockingReason: The version has to be chosen before the upload: once 0.1.0 is uploaded again, crates.io cannot undo the collision, and the maintainer's own Cargo cache already holds the withdrawn package.
findings.reproduction: Run `build/republished-version.sh <work>`. Offline, with a fresh `CARGO_HOME`, a local sparse registry on 127.0.0.1 serves a synthetic crate `probe` 0.1.0 that prints "withdrawn", and a consumer builds it; the registry then serves other bytes as 0.1.0, which print "republished", with their own checksum. `cargo update -p probe`, the remedy the CHANGELOG gave, is refused: "checksum for `probe v0.1.0 (registry `probe`)` changed between lock files". After `cargo generate-lockfile` the lockfile records the new checksum `21b0c5002a9e…`, yet the program prints "withdrawn", and so does a new consumer without a lockfile; the server log shows one download of the `.crate`. The challenge harness `skeptic-bld-republish/cache-cause.sh` shows that a plain `cargo update` is refused too, that deleting the extracted source only re-extracts the cached `.crate`, and that even after the cached `.crate` is deleted a kept target folder still runs the old code. The maintainer's Cargo cache holds the withdrawn `mhfe-core-0.1.0.crate`, SHA-256 `bc23d4d1dcdbdcef54100eb9a04cd6634ca37898ea1098e4385505724906269d`, crates.io answers 404 for `mhfe-core`, and `Cargo.toml:3` says `version = "0.1.0"`.
findings.expected: A published version names one package everywhere, the checksum in `Cargo.lock` identifies what is built, and the CHANGELOG's remedy, `cargo update -p mhfe-core`, renews a lockfile that recorded the withdrawn package.
findings.observed: Cargo keys its download cache, its extracted sources and its build outputs by name and version, and does not check a cached `.crate` against the checksum in the lockfile or the index. On a machine or mirror that fetched the withdrawn 0.1.0, a build that resolves the new 0.1.0 compiles the withdrawn source while `Cargo.lock` records the new checksum, and the documented remedy is refused. crates.io would accept the upload: its publish code checks only the 24-hour reserve on a deleted crate's name (crates.io `main` at `d21c1ec`, `publish.rs:162-174`), its team closed the pull request that would have refused versions of deleted crates (#10016), and Cargo issue #10071 on changed checksums is open.
findings.impact: Anyone who has the withdrawn 0.1.0 in a Cargo cache, a vendored registry or a mirror builds the withdrawn code under the new version's checksum. This includes the maintainer's machine, where a local program of the owner pins `=0.1.0` with the withdrawn checksum. Since the API changed, most such builds fail to compile against the old source, which is confusing; a consumer whose code compiles against both, or that keeps its old lockfile, runs the withdrawn draft code silently. Either way the lockfile no longer identifies what was compiled. No secret is exposed. An upload cannot be undone. mhfe at `67e0b4c` does not depend on mhfe-core yet; its plan adds the dependency in step M10.
findings.challenge: Confirmed, medium: the challenger reproduced it, isolated the caches involved, settled from crates.io's code that the upload would be accepted, and found the owner's local program that pins `=0.1.0`. Corrected: mhfe does not depend on mhfe-core yet, and cleaning the cache alone is not enough.
findings.recommendedFix: Release under a new version number before any upload: bump `Cargo.toml`, the root entry of `Cargo.lock` and the CHANGELOG heading (0.2.0 fits semantic versioning, since the API differs from the withdrawn 0.1.0), and replace the CHANGELOG paragraph about `cargo update -p mhfe-core` with one sentence saying that the release supersedes the withdrawn 0.1.0. Removing the stale entries from a Cargo cache is not enough on its own: a kept target folder still runs the old code.
findings.requiredVerification: Every place names one new version; the release workflow's notes step finds its section, which gives no `cargo update` advice; no other tracked file names 0.1.0; the package file list holds and `cargo package` writes the new version; no Cargo cache of the machine holds a package or index entry of the new version.

findings.title: An unbounded BIP39 passphrase makes Seed::derive and wallet_check::draw take time quadratic in a run of combining marks
findings.releaseBlockingReason: Low: availability of the user's own offline process on an input the host passes, with correct results and no disclosure.
findings.reportedBy: security reviewer (CHECK-SEC-007); reported independently by the protocol reviewer as a FUN finding (CHECK-API-004) and by the api reviewer as an API finding (CHECK-API-001). One root cause, so one ID.
findings.reproduction: Build the security harness and run `input-bounds`, or call `Seed::derive(&phrase, &format!("a{}", "\u{301}".repeat(65536)))`: one letter followed by 128 KiB of U+0301 COMBINING ACUTE ACCENT. `wallet_check::draw(passphrase, fill)` normalizes the passphrase the same way before its first fill. The protocol harness's `nfkd_cost.py`, the api probe `nfkd` and three challenge harnesses (`skeptic-sec-nfkd`, `skeptic-fun-nfkd`, `skeptic-api-nfkd`) measure the same.
findings.expected: Normalizing a passphrase costs time linear in its length, or n log n like unicode-normalization's own `nfkd()` iterator, which sorts each run of non-starters once. The specification puts no length limit on the passphrase `Q` (its README.md:754 at `6f7537e`: the password's byte-length restrictions do not apply to `Q`), so the core may not refuse a long one.
findings.observed: `Nfkd::write` runs `std::str::from_utf8` over the whole pending run of non-starters for every non-starter it adds (src/nfkd.rs:53-55); for a mark out of order, `insertion_point` also scans back and line 59 rotates the bytes after the insertion point. The cost is quadratic in the length of one run. Measured by the security reviewer, release build, median of three: 0.057, 0.221, 0.870 and 3.454 s at 16, 32, 64 and 128 KiB (3.97 per doubling), against 0.003 to 0.004 s for ASCII of the same lengths, so PBKDF2 is not the cause. Out of order (U+0301 U+0316 repeated) it took 5.36 s at 128 KiB, and alternating marks 55.7 s at 320 KB. Runs of 30 marks, the limit of Unicode's stream-safe format, stay linear. The seeds are correct. The code it was cut from, mhfe `67e0b4c` (src/wallet.rs:1074-1080), used the `nfkd()` iterator.
findings.impact: Availability only: no secret is exposed and no result is wrong. A passphrase read from a file, pasted, or passed by another program, with one run of tens of thousands of combining marks, holds the call for seconds; by extrapolation about 4 minutes at 1 MiB. Neither function can be cancelled while it normalizes; ending the process, which the specification allows, stops it. A typed line is not affected in practice: 4,096 marks in one run take 10 to 16 ms, and mhfe limits a typed line to 8 KiB. For `draw` the normalization runs once before about 65,536 PBKDF2 trials, so the added cost matters mainly for `Seed::derive`. MHFE passwords are not affected: `Password::new` counts first and refuses more than 1,024 bytes before it writes.
findings.challenge: Confirmed, low, by three challengers. Corrections taken into this record: the quadratic term of an in-order run is the `from_utf8` alone; stepping back one character at a time, or keeping the run's last class, fixes runs in canonical order only; the original harnesses measured in-order runs only, so the out-of-order case is recorded separately; "minutes" needs about 320 KB in one run of two classes.
findings.recommendedFix: Smallest change: keep the class of the run's last character, which is its largest; a starter, or a non-starter whose class is not below it, is written at the end with no validation and no search. A run in canonical order then costs linear time. Add a sentence to the docs of `Seed::derive` and `draw` that a run out of canonical order still costs quadratic time, so a host bounds a passphrase it reads from a file or the clipboard. The complete fix, sorting each run once when it ends with scratch space in a `Secret` as the dependency's iterator does, is more code; the owner's minimal-code rule chose the smaller change.

findings.title: NativeArgon2::argon2id cuts a password of 4 GiB or more to 32 bits and returns the tag of another password

findings.reproduction: Build the api probes and run `aud002-api-probes truncation`: `NativeArgon2::new(32)`, then `argon2id` with 2^32 + 1 zero bytes, a 16-byte salt, 32 KiB and one pass, and the same call with the first byte only. It prints `password of 4294967297 bytes: Ok(()); its tag equals that of the 1-byte password: true`. The challenge harness `skeptic-api-trunc` gives a password of exactly 2^32 bytes the tag of the empty password, after a control in which 2,000 bytes do not share the 1-byte tag.
findings.expected: The trait's contract (src/engine.rs:27-29) is the tag of `password`, or `OutOfMemory` or `Argon2Failed`. RFC 9106 allows at most 2^32 - 1 bytes, and the C code's own size_t entry points refuse a longer password with `ARGON2_PWD_TOO_LONG`. findings.observed: `ffi::argon2id` writes `pwdlen: inputs.password.len() as u32` (src/engine/ffi.rs:124), so the C code reads the length modulo 2^32 and returns `Ok` with the tag of a shorter password. findings.title: Every public function that clears the stack needs about 136 KiB of free stack and ends the process on a 128 KiB thread, which no document said
findings.releaseBlockingReason: Low: availability only, the default stacks of the tested targets suffice, and the fix is documentation.
findings.reproduction: Run `aud002-api-probes stack-floor`: each of `Phrase::read_word`, `Phrase::read`, `Password::new`, `Check::of`, `Seed::derive` and `wallet_check::draw` runs in a child process on threads of 64 to 256 KiB. In debug and release builds on x86-64 Linux with glibc each completes from 136 KiB and fails at 128 KiB. `Phrase::read_word` on 128 KiB ends with "stack overflow, aborting", exit 134. The challenge harness `skeptic-api-stack` shows that calls which do not clear the stack complete with about 123 KiB free on a 128 KiB thread, and that a `pthread_create` thread of 128 KiB, as a C host makes one, ends with SIGSEGV.
findings.expected: A public function runs on the platforms' ordinary thread stacks, or its documentation says what stack it needs (CORE-20).
findings.observed: `stack::cleared` overwrites a 128 KiB array below the caller's frame after every such call, so even an 8-byte word lookup needs about 136 KiB. The crate doc and the public rustdoc did not mention the clear; README.md:42-46 named only "a fixed depth"; SECURITY.md:25-28 named 128 KiB but no minimum stack and no abort.
findings.impact: A host thread of 128 KiB or less ends the whole process at the first such call, deterministically, so it shows in development and does not depend on data. musl's default thread stack is 128 KiB (from musl's source; not tested here). Rust threads get 2 MiB by default, glibc main threads usually 8 MiB, Apple secondary threads 512 KiB, Android and Windows threads 1 MiB. The crate has no C ABI, so a C or Go host on musl reaches it only through its own wrapper. Availability only.
findings.challenge: Confirmed, low. Corrected: the crate doc did not describe the clear at all, so the sentence had to be added there rather than repeated; the impact is narrower than first stated (Rust threads, no C ABI, deterministic failure).
findings.recommendedFix: One sentence in the crate doc, and the same in README.md and SECURITY.md: such a call needs about 140 KiB of free stack, and on a smaller thread stack, such as musl's default of 128 KiB, it ends the process. findings.reproduction: Run `docs/doc-claims.sh <withdrawn mhfe-core-0.1.0.crate>`: `withdrawn-release` fails with `licence features API`. The challenge harness `skeptic-doc-withdrawn/old-consumer.sh` builds two consumers written for the withdrawn package against this checkout: one asking for the feature `browser-core` fails with "failed to select a version for `mhfe-core`", and one importing `mhfe_core::{Completion, ErrorCode}` fails with E0432; exit 1.
findings.expected: Notes for a release that replaces a withdrawn one name every difference its users meet (DOC-001): code written for it does not build against this one, its features are gone, and the licence is MIT alone instead of MIT OR Apache-2.0.
findings.observed: The withdrawn package, which crates.io served from 2026-10-25, had the licence MIT OR Apache-2.0, seven features (`browser-core`, `browser-diagnostics`, `browser-normalization`, `browser-passwords`, `browser-repair`, `browser-wallet`, `wasm-bindings`) and 14 public modules with items such as `Completion`, `CallbackError` and `ErrorCode`. `dec9c81` is MIT, has no features and the 22 public items of `docs/public-api.txt`. CHANGELOG.md:10-12, which `release.yml` publishes as the release notes and the package ships, named only the new checksum and `cargo update -p mhfe-core`, which implies a drop-in replacement.
findings.impact: A user of the withdrawn package who follows the note gets a Cargo error for an unknown feature or compile errors for removed items, and the licence narrows without notice. The break shows at once as a build error; no secret is exposed and protocol output is untouched. The text is frozen into the package and the release notes when published.

findings.title: On Windows, no_core_dumps is documented as "a crash writes no core dump" while error reports still hold the threads' stacks
findings.releaseBlockingReason: Low documentation defect: the code applies what it intends, and the residue is transient stack data that only a crash on Windows exposes.
findings.reproduction: Read `src/os/windows.rs`: `enter()` changes error reporting only through `WerSetFlags(WER_FAULT_REPORTING_FLAG_NOHEAP)` (line 196), and `no_core_dumps` is that flag read back (line 226). Microsoft documents the flag as leaving heap information out of a crash report, and even a normal minidump keeps what stack traces of every thread need. `docs/doc-claims.sh` fails `no-core-dumps-field` and `windows-report-residue`, and passes on a copy with the two sentences changed; `skeptic-doc-wer/check-wer-claims.sh` prints five FAIL lines, exit 1.
findings.expected: The field doc and SECURITY.md promise on Windows only what the code does (DOC-07): error reports leave out the heap, the secret pages and the work area, and a report made after a crash still holds every thread's stack and registers.
findings.observed: The field doc opened with "A crash writes no core dump" for every system and grounded the Windows case only in "error reports leave out the heap". The Windows section of SECURITY.md, the Windows paragraph of `enter()`'s doc and README's Windows bullet never named what a report still holds, while the Android texts name the tombstone residue.
findings.impact: A host that shows `no_core_dumps == true` as "no core dumps" misleads its user on Windows. A crash during an operation leaves stack values, such as the `bip39` parsing and PBKDF2 states and copies the end-of-call stack clear has not yet overwritten, in a Windows Error Reporting report, which Windows queues and may send under the system's consent settings. The operating system can cause such a crash, for instance an allocation failure. Secret pages and the Argon2id work area are excluded and not affected. Not demonstrated on Windows: the finding rests on Microsoft's documentation.
findings.challenge: Confirmed, low. Added: `enter()`'s Windows "Not covered" list mirrors SECURITY.md and needs the same clause; a possible variant on macOS and iOS crash reports was not checked.
findings.recommendedFix: Documentation only: the field doc says that on Unix a crash writes no core dump and that on Windows error reports, which still hold the threads' stacks, leave out the heap; the Windows "Not covered" lists of `enter()`'s doc and SECURITY.md add the threads' stacks and registers that an error report still holds.
findings.requiredVerification: `doc-claims.sh` passes both checks and `check-wer-claims.sh` passes every check on the fixed tree; the code is unchanged.
